title: Antibiotics that attack the bacterial cell wall
ariaLabel: Schematic of bacterial cell wall building: precursors are made in the cytoplasm, carried across the membrane on a lipid carrier as lipid II, joined into glycan chains by transglycosylase, and cross-linked by transpeptidases (the penicillin-binding proteins) into a strong wall. Fosfomycin and cycloserine act on early precursors, bacitracin on the lipid carrier, vancomycin on the substrate of the later steps, and beta-lactams on the transpeptidase. A beta-lactamase destroys a beta-lactam, and a beta-lactamase inhibitor protects it.
caption: Schematic, not to scale. Flow and levels are qualitative and illustrative; no dose, concentration or MIC is shown or implied.

blockInfo: An antibiotic of the chosen class acting at this step (generic teaching symbol, not a named drug's shape). Less passes, so the wall behind it is built less. A growing cell with a weak wall swells and bursts in its own osmotic pressure.

nodes.label: Cytoplasmic precursors
nodes.info: Building blocks of the wall made in the bacterial cytoplasm: UDP-N-acetylglucosamine and UDP-N-acetylmuramic acid, with a pentapeptide ending in D-alanyl-D-alanine. The slider sets how fast the cell is growing.

nodes.label: Muramyl pentapeptide
nodes.info: UDP-muramyl pentapeptide: the finished building block. Its D-alanyl-D-alanine end is the part later steps and some antibiotics recognise.

nodes.label: Lipid II
nodes.info: Lipid II: the building block attached to a lipid carrier (bactoprenol) that carries it across the cell membrane to the growing wall. The carrier must be recycled to be used again.

nodes.label: Glycan chains
nodes.info: Glycan chains: transglycosylases join the sugar units of lipid II into long chains.

nodes.label: Cross-linked cell wall
nodes.info: Transpeptidases (the penicillin-binding proteins) cross-link the peptides of neighbouring chains into a strong net that resists the osmotic pressure inside the cell.

nodes.label: Cell lysis
nodes.info: Without a strong wall a growing bacterium swells and bursts. Wall-active antibiotics are therefore bactericidal against growing cells. Lysis here rises when less wall is built while the cell keeps growing.

edges.label: Mur enzymes
edges.info: Early cytoplasmic steps (the Mur enzymes). Fosfomycin blocks the first, MurA; cycloserine blocks alanine racemase and D-alanine ligase, which make the D-Ala-D-Ala end.

edges.label: lipid carrier
edges.info: Attachment to the lipid carrier and its recycling. Bacitracin blocks the dephosphorylation that recycles the carrier.

edges.label: transglycosylase
edges.info: Transglycosylation: joining sugar units into glycan chains. Vancomycin binds the D-Ala-D-Ala end of the building blocks and so blocks this step (and, by hiding the peptide, the cross-linking).

edges.label: transpeptidase (PBP)
edges.info: Transpeptidation by the penicillin-binding proteins. A beta-lactam resembles the D-Ala-D-Ala end and binds the enzyme's active site permanently, so cross-links are not made. A beta-lactamase breaks the beta-lactam ring first; a beta-lactamase inhibitor such as clavulanate stops it doing so.

sources: Beta-lactams. They block the final step of peptidoglycan assembly: they bind the penicillin-binding proteins (the transpeptidases), stop cross-linking, and the cell loses viability and lyses (Beta-lactam antibiotics, StatPearls).
Beta-lactamase inhibitors. Clavulanate-type agents are given with a beta-lactam to prevent resistance by inhibiting serine beta-lactamases (Beta-lactamase inhibitors, StatPearls).

Fosfomycin, cycloserine, bacitracin and vancomycin. Fosfomycin inhibits MurA, cycloserine the enzymes making D-alanyl-D-alanine, bacitracin the recycling of the lipid carrier, and vancomycin binds the D-Ala-D-Ala end of the precursors. These are standard teaching in the pharmacology texts the PrepNucleus lessons cite (Katzung; KD Tripathi) and were not checked against a linked source here, so they are flagged for review.
simplified: The Gram-negative outer membrane and porins, efflux pumps, altered penicillin-binding proteins (MRSA), other beta-lactamases (ESBL, carbapenemases, metallo-enzymes), vancomycin resistance by D-Ala-D-Lac, autolysins, the tolerance of non-growing cells, and the differences between penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems and monobactams are left out. Lysis is drawn as the opposite of wall strength in a growing cell. Levels, flow and the size of each block are illustrative. The drug choices are teaching toggles of a class: no named drug, dose or schedule is shown or implied, and the figure does not say who should or should not take any of them.
